description: Hot and Sour Soup is a beloved Chinese classic, known for its exhilarating balance of spicy chili, tangy vinegar, and savory umami flavors. This comforting soup, often brimming with tender pork, tofu, mushrooms, and bamboo shoots, offers a delightful warmth with every spoonful. It is a perfect starter or a light meal, embodying the rich culinary heritage of China.

instructions.title: Prepare Ingredients
instructions.text: Rehydrate dried shiitake and wood ear mushrooms in hot water for 20 minutes, then squeeze dry and slice thinly. Slice pork loin into thin strips and marinate with a pinch of salt and white pepper. Cut tofu and bamboo shoots into matchsticks.

instructions.title: Build the Broth Base
instructions.text: In a large pot, bring chicken or vegetable broth to a boil. Add the sliced pork and cook until just done, about 2-3 minutes. Skim any foam from the surface.

instructions.title: Add Vegetables and Seasonings
instructions.text: Stir in the rehydrated shiitake mushrooms, wood ear mushrooms, and bamboo shoots. Bring back to a simmer. Add rice vinegar, soy sauce, dark soy sauce, white pepper, and chili oil. Taste and adjust seasonings as needed.

instructions.title: Thicken the Soup
instructions.text: Slowly pour the cornstarch slurry into the simmering soup while stirring continuously until the soup thickens to your desired consistency. This usually takes a few minutes.

instructions.title: Incorporate Egg and Tofu
instructions.text: Reduce heat to low. Slowly drizzle the beaten egg into the soup in a thin stream, stirring gently with chopsticks or a fork to create delicate egg ribbons. Add the tofu matchsticks and stir gently.

instructions.title: Finish and Serve
instructions.text: Stir in the sesame oil. Ladle the hot soup into individual bowls. Garnish generously with chopped green onions. Serve immediately and enjoy the authentic flavors.

tips: For an extra layer of flavor, use homemade chicken stock. Adjust the amount of vinegar and white pepper to your personal preference for spiciness and tanginess.
If you can't find wood ear mushrooms, fresh shiitake mushrooms can be used, though the texture will be slightly different. For a vegetarian version, omit pork and use vegetable broth.
Hot and Sour Soup is best served immediately. Leftovers can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 2 days; reheat gently on the stove, adding a splash of broth if it's too thick.
article:
Unveiling the fiery and tangy allure of Chinese cuisine, Hot and Sour Soup stands as a testament to the intricate balance of flavors that defines this rich culinary tradition. More than just a starter, this iconic dish is a symphony of textures and tastes, celebrated worldwide for its invigorating kick and comforting depth. Whether you're a seasoned chef or a curious home cook, mastering the art of Hot and Sour Soup promises a rewarding culinary journey that brings the authentic flavors of China right into your kitchen.

## What is Hot and Sour Soup?
Hot and Sour Soup, or "Suan La Tang" in Mandarin, is a quintessential Chinese soup known for its distinctive two-pronged flavor profile: a spicy heat ("hot") and a sharp tang ("sour"). Originating from Sichuan cuisine, it has evolved into a beloved staple across various regions of China and beyond, with countless regional variations. The "hot" typically comes from white pepper and chili oil, while the "sour" is predominantly derived from rice vinegar. Beyond these core elements, the soup is a medley of ingredients, often including shredded pork, mushrooms (shiitake, wood ear), bamboo shoots, tofu, and egg drops, all suspended in a thickened, savory broth. The interplay of earthy mushrooms, tender protein, crunchy bamboo, and silky tofu creates a complex textural experience that is just as captivating as its vibrant flavor. It’s a soup designed to awaken the palate, offering warmth and a burst of zest in every spoonful.

## Ingredients You Need
Crafting an authentic Hot and Sour Soup requires a thoughtful selection of ingredients. Here's a breakdown of what you'll need to bring this classic dish to life:

*   **For the Broth:**
    *   6 cups chicken or vegetable broth (low sodium preferred)
    *   2 tablespoons soy sauce (light)
    *   1 tablespoon dark soy sauce (for color and depth)
    *   1 tablespoon sesame oil
    *   1 teaspoon white pepper (crucial for the "hot")
    *   1/4 cup rice vinegar (essential for the "sour," adjust to taste)
    *   1 tablespoon chili oil (optional, for extra heat)

*   **Main Fillings:**
    *   4 oz pork loin or tenderloin, thinly sliced or shredded (substitute with chicken, shrimp, or extra tofu for vegetarian)
    *   4 oz firm tofu, pressed and cut into small strips or cubes
    *   1/2 cup dried shiitake mushrooms, rehydrated and thinly sliced (reserve soaking liquid for broth)
    *   1/2 cup dried wood ear mushrooms, rehydrated and thinly sliced
    *   1/2 cup bamboo shoots, thinly sliced (canned or fresh)

*   **Thickening & Finishing:**
    *   3 tablespoons cornstarch mixed with 4 tablespoons cold water (cornstarch slurry)
    *   2 large eggs, lightly beaten
    *   2 green onions, thinly sliced (for garnish)

## Step-by-Step Instructions
Making Hot and Sour Soup is an enjoyable process that yields delicious results. Follow these steps for a perfect bowl:

1.  **Prepare Ingredients:** Rehydrate dried mushrooms by soaking them in hot water for at least 30 minutes. Once soft, drain, squeeze out excess water, and slice thinly. If using shiitake, strain and reserve the soaking liquid to add to your broth for extra umami. Thinly slice your pork, tofu, and bamboo shoots. Prepare your cornstarch slurry and beat your eggs.
2.  **Sauté Aromatics (Optional):** In a large pot or Dutch oven, heat a tablespoon of oil over medium heat. If using pork, you can quickly stir-fry it until it's just cooked through, then remove and set aside. This step adds an extra layer of flavor.
3.  **Build the Broth:** Pour the chicken or vegetable broth into the pot. Add the reserved shiitake mushroom liquid (if using). Bring the broth to a simmer.
4.  **Add Main Fillings:** Once simmering, add the sliced shiitake mushrooms, wood ear mushrooms, and bamboo shoots to the broth. Let them cook for about 5 minutes to infuse their flavors.
5.  **Season the Soup:** Stir in the soy sauce, dark soy sauce, sesame oil, and white pepper. If you stir-fried the pork, add it back to the pot now. Add the tofu. Taste the broth and adjust seasonings as needed. This is where you can add chili oil if desired.
6.  **Thicken the Soup:** Slowly pour the cornstarch slurry into the simmering soup in a thin stream, stirring constantly to prevent lumps. Continue stirring until the soup thickens to your desired consistency. It should be slightly viscous but not overly gloopy.
7.  **Add Egg Drops:** Once the soup has thickened, slowly drizzle the beaten eggs into the hot, swirling soup. Use a fork or chopsticks to gently stir the soup as you pour, creating beautiful, delicate egg ribbons. Cook for about 30 seconds until the egg is set.
8.  **Final Touches:** Remove the soup from the heat. Stir in the rice vinegar. Taste again and adjust the "hot" (more white pepper or chili oil) and "sour" (more vinegar) to your preference. Remember, the vinegar's flavor is best when added at the end.
9.  **Serve:** Ladle the Hot and Sour Soup into bowls and garnish generously with sliced green onions.

## Pro Tips for the Best Results
To truly elevate your Hot and Sour Soup, consider these expert tips:

*   **Balance is Key:** The essence of Hot and Sour Soup lies in the perfect equilibrium between its spicy, tangy, savory, and umami notes. Don't be afraid to taste and adjust the white pepper, vinegar, and soy sauce multiple times at the end. A little extra of one can dramatically change the profile.
*   **Quality Ingredients:** Use good quality broth, fresh mushrooms (or well-rehydrated dried ones), and firm tofu. The better your foundational ingredients, the more robust your soup will be.
*   **White Pepper Power:** White pepper is paramount for the authentic "hot" flavor. Black pepper offers a different kind of heat and won't give the same characteristic taste. Don't skimp on it!
*   **Vinegar Timing:** Add the rice vinegar at the very end, off the heat. Cooking vinegar for too long can mellow its acidity, diminishing its vibrant tang.
*   **Cornstarch Slurry Control:** Always mix your cornstarch with cold water before adding it to hot liquid to prevent lumps. Add it gradually, stirring constantly, until you reach your desired thickness. You might not need all of it.
*   **Egg Drop Technique:** For perfect, feathery egg ribbons, ensure your soup is at a gentle simmer, not a rolling boil. Pour the egg slowly from a height while gently stirring the soup in one direction.

## Serving Suggestions
Hot and Sour Soup is a versatile dish that can be enjoyed in many ways. It makes an excellent appetizer for any Chinese meal, pairing beautifully with dishes like General Tso's chicken, Kung Pao shrimp, or vegetable lo mein. For a lighter meal, it can stand alone as a satisfying lunch, perhaps accompanied by a simple side of steamed rice or a fresh spring roll. Garnish with extra green onions, a drizzle of chili oil for those who crave more heat, or a dash of extra white pepper. Some even enjoy it with a sprinkle of crispy fried shallots or wonton strips for added texture.

## Variations and Substitutions
The beauty of Hot and Sour Soup lies in its adaptability. Don't hesitate to experiment with variations or make substitutions based on dietary needs or what you have on hand:

*   **Vegetarian/Vegan:** Omit the pork and use vegetable broth. For an extra protein boost, increase the amount of tofu or add rehydrated textured vegetable protein (TVP). Ensure your soy sauce is vegan-friendly.
*   **Protein Alternatives:** Instead of pork, try shredded chicken breast, thinly sliced beef, or even shrimp (add shrimp in the last few minutes of cooking to prevent overcooking).
*   **Mushroom Medley:** Explore other mushroom varieties like enoki, button, or oyster mushrooms for different textures and flavors.
*   **Vegetable Boost:** Feel free to add other thinly sliced vegetables such as carrots, water chestnuts, or snow peas for extra crunch and nutrition.
*   **Spice Level:** Adjust the white pepper and chili oil to your personal preference. For a milder soup, reduce the amounts; for more fire, increase them or add a pinch of dried red chili flakes.
*   **Gluten-Free:** Use tamari instead of regular soy sauce and ensure your broth is gluten-free.

Hot and Sour Soup is more than just a soup; it's an experience. Its dynamic flavors, comforting warmth, and satisfying textures make it a beloved dish across cultures. By following these guidelines and embracing the spirit of culinary adventure, you can recreate this Chinese classic in your own kitchen, delighting your senses with every hot and sour, savory spoonful. So, gather your ingredients, fire up your stove, and prepare to embark on a flavorful journey that will undoubtedly become a staple in your cooking repertoire.
